issues.body: bench_s3_trust_allows_ec2 returns success upon finding any matching Allow statement, without evaluating an overriding Deny or a Condition that excludes the launched instances. When python3 is unavailable, any occurrence of ec2.amazonaws.com passes, including a Deny statement or a statement with the wrong action. cmd_check then says the policy lets EC2 call sts:AssumeRole and reports READY, while scripts/bench/README.md promises READY only when EC2 can actually assume the role. Merely documenting the helper as a partial drift detector does not make those externally visible readiness claims true. The round-3 counterexamples also remain untested.
issues.fix_hint: Because provision owns and overwrites this role, fail closed unless the parsed trust document is equivalent to the canonical bench_s3_trust_policy, or implement the relevant IAM Deny and Condition semantics. If no real JSON parser is available, withhold READY instead of using a substring test. Add hermetic cases for Allow plus overriding Deny, Allow with an incompatible Condition, and the no-python path; all must make check return nonzero and omit READY.
issues.title: Trust check still reports READY for policies that can deny EC2 assumption

verdict.summary: Round 4 leaves the round-3 load-bearing trust-validation defect unchanged. bench_s3_trust_allows_ec2 still accepts the first matching Allow without accounting for an overriding Deny or an incompatible Condition, and its no-python branch still accepts any document containing the EC2 service substring. The new comments now acknowledge that this is only a partial drift detector, but cmd_check and the README continue to make the stronger claim that READY means the trust policy actually lets EC2 assume the role. The added tests cover only wrong/missing principals and do not exercise the previously requested Deny, Condition, or no-parser counterexamples. This is materially the same major finding, so progress is stagnant.
